what: Kratos Defense builds unmanned systems and defence electronics. Its products include jet-powered target drones that air forces shoot at in training, low-cost combat drones designed to fly alongside crewed aircraft, satellite ground systems, hypersonic test vehicles and rocket propulsion.
customers: The United States Air Force, Navy and Army, allied governments, and prime defence contractors who integrate Kratos systems into larger programmes.
money: Target drones, tactical jet drones and the collaborative combat aircraft programmes.
Satellite ground systems, microwave electronics, rocket propulsion, hypersonic vehicles and training systems.
moat: Kratos has spent years building jet-powered drones at a fraction of the cost of crewed aircraft, and that cost position is now exactly what the United States Air Force wants as it moves toward attritable aircraft that can be risked or lost. Being already qualified on target drone programmes gave it flight-test experience that competitors starting now do not have.
risks: Reported net income of $22.0M on $1.6B of revenue, a price/earnings ratio of 247 and 50.7 times EV/EBITDA — the valuation is entirely about future programmes, not current earnings.
Free cash flow of about negative $123.0M, as the company invests ahead of programme awards.
Twenty-five analysts average a $74.68 target against a $29.65 price, a gap of over 150% that indicates extraordinary disagreement about programme outcomes.
Defence procurement decisions determine everything here, and a programme that goes to a competitor leaves years of investment stranded.
Well-funded private competitors including Anduril are pursuing the same programmes with more capital and fewer legacy costs.
opportunities: Revenue has grown consistently, from $811.5M in 2021 to $1.3B in 2025, with trailing revenue of $1.6B.
Cash of $560.6M against only $46.6M of debt is an unusually clean balance sheet for a company investing this heavily.
Attritable unmanned aircraft are a genuine strategic priority for the United States Air Force, and Kratos has flight-tested hardware rather than concepts.
The target drone business is a steady, long-running programme that funds the more speculative work.
Satellite ground systems and hypersonic test work are separate growth areas with their own funding streams.
watch: Programme awards and backlog. Nothing on the income statement describes this company’s prospects; which contracts it wins does.
view: Kratos is a bet on a change in how air forces think about aircraft, and the bet is not subtle. For decades, military aircraft have become more capable and far more expensive, to the point where losing one is a strategic event. The emerging doctrine is the opposite: large numbers of cheap unmanned aircraft that can be risked, flown alongside crewed fighters, and lost without consequence. Kratos has been building jet-powered drones cheaply for years because that is what target drone programmes required, and that experience is now exactly what the Air Force wants.

The financial statements say nothing useful. Net income of $22 million on $1.6 billion of revenue, a price/earnings ratio of 247, 50.7 times EV/EBITDA and negative free cash flow of $123 million. This is a company spending ahead of programme awards, which is the correct thing to do if you believe the awards are coming and a wealth-destroying thing to do if they are not. Cash of $561 million against $47 million of debt means it can afford to keep spending, and that balance sheet is genuinely the most reassuring thing about the position.

The twenty-five analysts averaging $74.68 against a $29.65 share price is the widest disagreement I have seen on a company this size, and it reflects the structure of the opportunity rather than confusion. These are binary programme outcomes: win the collaborative combat aircraft work and the valuation is low; lose it and years of investment is stranded. There is no middle outcome to model, so the analysts are averaging two very different scenarios.

What concerns me most is the competition, not the doctrine. Anduril and General Atomics are pursuing the same programmes, and Anduril in particular has more capital, no legacy cost base and a great deal of political attention. Kratos’s advantage is flight-tested hardware and existing qualification; that is real but it is not insurmountable. This is a venture-style position inside a listed defence company, and it should be sized that way. Programme awards and backlog are the only numbers worth following.
bull: Collaborative combat aircraft programmes go to Kratos on the strength of flight-tested, genuinely cheap hardware, turning years of investment into multi-year production revenue.
bear: Awards go to Anduril or General Atomics, years of pre-investment is stranded, and a company earning $22 million trades at 247 times earnings with nothing to fall back on.
